sequences.source_document: Published paper (PDF) with XML abstract and captions

steps.action: Take the prediction of Wiesmayr and Grasemann (2005) low-strain models: transtensional flanking structures should exist, and transtension favours a- and s-type flanking folds and impedes shear bands.
steps.quote: transtensional flanking structures must also exist in nature

steps.action: Compute mean annual velocities and strain-rate tensors from ZAMG dGPS stake positions (July 2018 to July 2019) by triangulating stakes (Appendix B).
steps.quote: Annual position measurements of a stake network were utilized to determine mean annual velocities and strain rates

steps.action: Map the study area in the summers of 2016-2020 with drone structure-from-motion photogrammetry (DEM and orthomosaic, Appendix A) and measure orientations with field techniques.
steps.quote: mapping was carried out with the aid of high-resolution drone photogrammetry

steps.action: Map crevasse sets and identify a predominant set of splaying crevasses that curve into longitudinal crevasses towards the centreline; cross-check their orientation against stake-derived maximum shortening orientations.
steps.quote: The predominant set comprises splaying crevasses

steps.action: Compare the splaying crevasse pattern with Nye's (1952) model, which predicts this geometry under longitudinal compression.
steps.quote: This crevasse pattern is consistent with Nye’s model that predicts this geometry in the presence of a longitudinal compressive stress

steps.action: Map foliation s1 and s2 (nested-spoon geometry; sub-vertical s2 at the left/central flow unit boundary), which serves as the passive marker.
steps.quote: The foliation is the most prominent fabric element in the study area

steps.action: Map and classify 159 flanking structures along the right margin of the left flow unit (a-type and s-type folds; measure offset, bulge κ and angle φ). Check fold cylindricity with π-axes. Note that only three CEs are inclined against flow and that no shear bands occur; interacting CE sets are left undescribed.
steps.quote: The majority of isolated flanking structures can be classified as reverse drag a-type, normal drag s-type or reverse drag s-type flanking folds

steps.action: State in the interim summary that morphology, flow field and structures indicate a near-surface transtensional flow regime caused by valley widening and decreasing bed slope.
steps.quote: consistent with a near-surface transtensional flow regime

steps.action: Derive the instantaneous CE behaviour under plane-strain transpression and transtension with Mohr circles. Under transtension the fabric attractor is oblique, shear bands are unstable and s-type folds dominate at large strain.
steps.quote: The dominant presence of s-type flanking folds and the absence of shear bands may hence be indicative for high-strain transtensional shear zones.

steps.action: Run semi-analytical modified-Eshelby models of a frictionless CE in a linear viscous matrix under transtension for five vorticities and three initial CE orientations to γ = 2.
steps.quote: modelled using an Eshelby solution, modified for viscous fluid modelling

steps.action: Vary the kinematic vorticity across the model series and find that the final geometry depends mainly on the initial CE orientation, not on Wk.
steps.quote: not very sensitive to the Wk of the imposed deformation

steps.action: Compare the natural structures with the modelled ones and list diagnostic features: s-type folds with φ > 45°, central reverse drag passing into normal drag at the tips, and no shear bands.
steps.quote: The natural flanking structures (Fig. 5) share many similarities with the modelled structures (Fig. 7)

steps.action: Exclude transpression for the mapped zone: a-type folds coexisting with shear bands would be diagnostic of transpression, and no shear band is present.
steps.quote: the mapped area of the Pasterze glacier does not contain a single shear band

steps.action: Optimise a reference line by maximising correlation, regress CE inclination φ on transverse distance (N = 155, p = 7.72e-18), and, assuming stable CE orientations, infer α, kinematic vorticity and ISA2 inclination as functions of distance.
steps.quote: it is possible to determine the vorticity

steps.action: Test the inferred ISA2 orientation against independently traced crevasses (N = 2409). It gives an upper bound to crevasse inclination, a pure-shear line where splaying crevasses become longitudinal, and an integrated ISA2 trajectory that matches the splaying crevasses.
steps.quote: the estimated upper bound for the crevasse orientations matches the splaying crevasses

steps.action: Reject Nye's parallel-sided-valley compressive flow as the cause: it fits the crevasses but not the transverse extension recorded by the flanking structures.
steps.quote: it is inconsistent with the progressive transtensional deformation recorded by the flanking structures

steps.action: Build a plane-strain kinematic model of a widening channel (uniform plus parabolic radial velocity) and compute eigenvector and ISA2 trajectories, finite strain ellipses and the vorticity distribution (Appendix D).
steps.quote: a kinematic model that qualitatively encompasses the superficial velocity distribution of a glacier shall suffice

steps.action: Compare the widening-channel model with the observed structures and the inferred transverse vorticity variation.
steps.quote: it is qualitatively consistent with the observed structures and the transverse variations of kinematic vorticity

steps.action: Explain the absence of map-view flanking structures further NE by sub-horizontal rotation axes, supported by flanking structures with sub-horizontal fold axes on longitudinal crevasse walls near the terminus.
steps.quote: Such flanking structures were indeed exposed on the fracture walls of longitudinal crevasses

steps.action: Check the stable-orientation premise of the estimation: compute CE rotation through time with Eq. 6 (Fig. 11) and compare the expected translation distances with the down-glacier distribution of CE orientations.
steps.quote: This crude estimate is consistent with the CE orientation vs. down-glacier distance plot

steps.action: Compare transtensional (Spiti, Himalaya) and transpressional (Schneeberg, Eastern Alps) s-type flanking folds in rock with the models and the Pasterze examples to set diagnostic criteria.
steps.quote: Note that some s-type flanking folds in the Pasterze (Fig. 5g and h) exhibit the same features.

steps.action: Pose the open question whether transtensional flow in the crust is rare or whether shear zone kinematics have been misinterpreted.
steps.quote: Is transtensional flow in the Earth’s crust rare or were the kinematics of certain shear zones misinterpreted?

steps.action: Keep the claim that the structures record plane-strain transtensional sub-simple shear caused mainly by down-glacier valley widening.
steps.quote: consistent with two-dimensional transtensional sub-simple shear caused by down-glacier valley widening

end.claim: The flanking fold geometries, absence of shear bands, spatial variation of CE orientations and splaying crevasses in the Pasterze are consistent with two-dimensional transtensional sub-simple shear caused by down-glacier valley widening.

decisive_move.sentence: Comparing the mapped flanking structures with Eshelby-model predictions under transtension, including the diagnostic absence of shear bands, is what turns the field description into a transtension claim.

gates.evidence: Action: the paper cites the theoretical expectation (Wiesmayr and Grasemann 2005) as motivation, but it does not say this prediction directed the 2016-2020 mapping; that is inference. Claim: transtension could have been contradicted by shear bands or by a mismatch with the crevasse orientations, but the paper reports consistency rather than a stated pass/fail test. Registration: nothing is reported as fixed before the data; the reference line was optimised on the data.

imports.item: Eshelby (1959) solution for the field outside an ellipsoidal inclusion, adapted to viscous flow
MATLAB adaptive ODE solver ode45 for material advection
Structure-from-Motion with drone imagery (Agisoft Metashape, PIX4Dcapture)
Mohr circles of the first and second kind for flow tensors
Jeffery-Hamel diverging channel flow (named, not used analytically)

novelty_claims.quote: Nearly all published examples of flanking structures are interpreted to have formed either under simple shear or [...]
To date, the only and most convincing example of a transtensional s-type flanking fold from a fold-and-thrust belt

limits: The supplied XML holds only the abstract and captions, so body steps are located by PDF page. No review file was supplied: the history of revisions is not visible, although the received/revised dates show a revision, and there is no review sequence. Sub-claims: the vorticity and ISA2 profile across the margin is an estimate that depends on the assumption of stable CE orientations (estimate_with_resolution at most; only regression confidence belts are given). The diagnostic criteria separating transtensional from transpressional flanking structures (no shear bands; s-type folds at φ > 45°; reverse-to-normal drag) are a regularity_in_range derived from the models. The attribution of splaying crevasses to ISA2-parallel nucleation is best_explanation. The models use linear viscous rheology while the paper states ice follows power-law creep (n = 3); the effect of this mismatch is not tested (inference). The stake network is sparse, and two strain rates are acknowledged as possibly inconsistent. Model-to-nature agreement is qualitative; no misfit metric is reported. The 3D nature of glacier flow is declared beyond scope. Classification of structures and selection of 'isolated' CEs involve unquantified judgement (inference).

disagreements.target: Nye (1952), p. 91, on the effect of down-glacier valley widening
disagreements.support: Using Nye's own compressive-flow condition, the authors argue that valley widening leads to longitudinal compression, the opposite of Nye's statement.
disagreements.quote: it is enigmatic why Nye (1952), on p. 91, states the opposite

disagreements.target: Nye's (1952) compressive flow model for a parallel-sided valley as explanation of the Pasterze structures
disagreements.support: The model fits the splaying crevasses but cannot produce the transverse extension recorded by the flanking structures, so the authors use a widening-channel kinematic model instead.
disagreements.quote: it is inconsistent with the progressive transtensional deformation recorded by the flanking structures

disagreements.target: Community view that most ductile shear zones record transpression (e.g., Xypolias 2010 and cited strain analyses)
disagreements.support: The natural and modelled transtensional flanking structures give criteria that might reveal misinterpreted transtensional shear zones; the authors raise this as a possibility, not a demonstration.
disagreements.quote: perhaps transtensional shear zones have been misinterpreted
